conflicts.issue: East Club Gateway Voluntary Annexation and General Commercial Zoning (Z220062 / BDG220031)
conflicts.summary: Council split 2-4 over whether to annex 13.96 acres at East Club Boulevard and I-85 for a Commercial General textual development plan, weighing Transit Opportunity Area design standards and Comprehensive Plan fidelity against applying current UDO rules for a local developer.
conflicts.side_a_position: Deny the annexation and rezoning because the textual development plan falls short of Comprehensive Plan Transit Opportunity Area standards and leaves multifamily housing unprohibited.
side_a_arguments: Under Commercial General zoning without a housing prohibition, up to 90 residential units could still be built without addressing site constraints.
The proposal lacks strong urban design commitments beyond a partial build-to zone and could result in an auto-oriented strip center with a sea of parking inconsistent with the TOA place type.
Missing August Planning Commission comments and the need to uphold the newly adopted Comprehensive Plan ahead of the UDO rewrite warranted a no vote.
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve the annexation and rezoning as consistent with current UDO rules and the future Place Type Map.
side_b_arguments: The site is designated Transit Opportunity Area on the future place type map, and the applicant cannot use downtown design districts in the suburban tier until the UDO is rewritten.
Gander Development is a small, two-year-old local firm that offered an extensive list of prohibited nuisance uses, a perimeter fence, and a $15,000 affordable housing contribution.
Council should apply existing rules consistently rather than making anticipatory rulings against smaller local developers.
conflicts.resolution: Motion 1 for voluntary annexation and the utility extension agreement failed 2-4, ending consideration of the rezoning.

conflicts.issue: Three-Month Contract Extension for ShotSpotter / SoundThinking Pilot
conflicts.summary: Council split 2-4 over whether to pay SoundThinking $52,356 to keep ShotSpotter active for three months while the Wilson Center completes its independent evaluation of the 12-month pilot.
conflicts.side_a_position: Let the pilot contract expire as scheduled and await the Wilson Center evaluation before making any further commitment.
side_a_arguments: Extending the contract for three months yields no new evaluation data because the Wilson Center study only covers the completed 12-month pilot.
Community speakers cited false positives, missed shootings, and lack of proven crime reduction.
Resources should prioritize preventative community investments and evidence-based evaluation.
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve the $52,356 three-month extension to maintain continuity of gunfire detection until the Wilson Center report arrives in March.
side_b_arguments: Funds were already available within the Police Department budget and cutting service mid-review leaves shooting victims without alerts when 911 is not called.
Families and residents in high-gunfire areas reported valuing faster police response and recovered shell casings.
Keeping sensors active avoids operational disruption if Council decides to continue after reviewing the report.
conflicts.resolution: Motion failed 2-4, terminating the ShotSpotter alert service upon expiration of the 12-month contract pending the Wilson Center report.

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Durham City Council Meeting - Ward 3 Vacancy Jan 16 2024
conflicts.issue: Ward 3 Vacancy Candidate Selection and Ranked-Choice Voting vs. Special Election
conflicts.summary: Council deadlocked 3-3 between Legal Aid housing attorney Chelsea Cook and attorney/community leader Sheila Huggins, sparking a procedural debate over whether to break the tie via ranked-choice voting or trigger a special election.
conflicts.side_a_position: Appoint Chelsea Cook (and support ranked-choice voting to resolve council deadlocks rather than defaulting to a special election).
side_a_arguments: Chelsea Cook brings deep expertise in affordable housing, eviction defense, and tenants' rights from Legal Aid that complements the dais.

DeDreana Freeman, Carl Rist, and Nate Baker argued ranked-choice voting offers a constructive compromise mechanism to select a broadly acceptable candidate when no one reaches four first-choice votes.
conflicts.side_b_position: Appoint Sheila Huggins as 'day-one ready,' and reject ranked-choice voting as an improper effort to avoid an election.
side_b_arguments: Sheila Huggins demonstrated mastery of city departments and prior council decisions during interviews and had previously earned thousands of Durham votes.

Mark-Anthony Middleton stated he had no second choice and argued Council's charter duty is to make a good-faith effort, not to use ranked-choice voting to avoid returning the seat to voters in a special election.
conflicts.resolution: Nate Baker shifted his vote from Huggins to Cook to reach a 4-2 majority; Mark-Anthony Middleton then changed his vote to Cook as an act of goodwill and Mayor Williams declared the appointment unanimous.

conflicts.issue: Racial Equity Commission Appointment vs. Re-Advertisement for Professional Experience (Item 2)
conflicts.summary: DeDreana Freeman sought to re-advertise a Racial Equity Commission vacancy to recruit candidates with professional racial equity experience, while Mark-Anthony Middleton opposed revisiting a consensus work-session selection.
conflicts.side_a_position: Re-advertise the appointment to recruit applicants with professional racial equity expertise.
side_a_arguments: As an advisory body to Council, the Racial Equity Commission would benefit from members possessing professional experience in racial equity.
conflicts.side_b_position: Proceed with the scheduled vote on the volunteer applicant already selected by work-session consensus.
side_b_arguments: The proper time to request re-advertisement was during the work session rather than at the regular meeting after the applicant's name became public.
Pulling or rejecting the nomination at this stage risks sending an unfair message that the volunteer resident is deficient or unfit.
conflicts.resolution: Council proceeded to a formal vote and approved the appointment 5-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting no.

conflicts.issue: Page Road / Greenwood Annexation and 70-Townhome Rezoning Without On-Site Affordable Units
conflicts.summary: While four members approved the Page Road / Greenwood annexation and rezoning after the developer doubled its housing fund proffer to $35,000, two members voted no due to the absence of on-site affordable units.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve annexation and PDR 7.827 rezoning for up to 70 townhouses with an increased $35,000 dedicated housing fund proffer.
side_a_arguments: The project adds needed townhome housing supply contiguous to city services and aligns with the mixed residential neighborhood place type.
The developer doubled its dedicated housing fund contribution from $17,500 to $35,000.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the rezoning and annexation because the development lacks on-site affordable units.
side_b_arguments: New townhome developments in Durham should include actual affordable units rather than relying solely on modest cash proffers.
A no vote signals to other developers that stronger affordability commitments are expected.
conflicts.resolution: Both the annexation/UEA and zoning map amendment passed 4-2, and the consistency statement passed 6-0.

conflicts.issue: Conservation Subdivisions UDO Text Amendment Amid Pending Appellate Litigation
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether to adopt an expedited UDO amendment clarifying that conservation subdivisions need only meet §6.2.4.H objective standards rather than all 12 general purposes in §6.2.4.A while a lawsuit against Durham County is before the Court of Appeals.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the clarifying text amendment immediately to align the UDO with 15 years of planning practice and insulate the City from litigation.
side_a_arguments: Reading §6.2.4.A's 12 aspirational purposes as mandatory makes conservation subdivisions legally impossible to approve.
Objective, measurable criteria in §6.2.4.H protect primary conservation areas without exposing the City to lawsuits.
Stronger environmental protections in Falls Lake and Southeast Durham were addressed through phased grading and belong in the UDO rewrite.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the amendment over environmental enforcement concerns in Southeast Durham and dissatisfaction with removing purpose-statement safeguards.
side_b_arguments: Existing conservation subdivisions in Southeast Durham have caused severe sediment runoff into waterways.
Modifying the purpose-statement language before the Court of Appeals rules does not adequately strengthen environmental protection.
conflicts.resolution: The UDO text amendment passed 5-1 (DeDreana Freeman opposed), and the consistency statement passed 6-0.

conflicts.issue: Oaks at Gray Townhome Rezoning Density Bonus and Neighborhood Compatibility (321-325 Gray Ave)
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-2 over whether to rezone 0.435 acres in a predominantly single-family gentrifying neighborhood to allow eight market-rate townhouses instead of the five permitted by right.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the eight-townhouse rezoning as smaller, more attainable infill housing with off-street garage parking.
side_a_arguments: Building eight smaller 1,600-1,800 sq ft units yields lower price points than five larger townhomes allowed by right.
The project provides infill housing near downtown with garages and a small parking lot to address street parking concerns.
Local resident developers are investing in their first triangle project.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose granting three extra units by rezoning without using affordable housing density bonuses or single-family design commitments.
side_b_arguments: Granting extra units via rezoning undermines incentives for developers to use affordable housing density bonuses.
The property lies in a gentrifying neighborhood where $500k-$600k townhomes do not serve existing residents and exacerbate displacement.
The textual plan lacked design commitments to fit a predominantly single-family street and departed from the Established Residential place type.
conflicts.resolution: The zoning map change passed 4-2, and the consistency statement passed 5-1 (Nate Baker opposed).

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Jan 4, 2024
conflicts.issue: Procedural Pathway for Small Area Planning (Council Work Session Resolution vs. JCCPC Referral)
conflicts.summary: Council members differed over whether to initiate a small area planning discussion—including Walltown and Northgate Mall—directly on a City Council work session agenda or route it first through the Joint City-County Planning Committee (JCCPC).
conflicts.side_a_position: Bring the small area planning discussion or resolution to a City Council work session so all council members can provide input early.
side_a_arguments: Nate Baker noted rules of procedure were unclear and wanted a work session discussion on small area planning beyond just Northgate Mall within a feasible staff timeline.
Carl Rist noted he was no longer on JCCPC and wanted an opportunity for his voice to be heard at a full Council work session.
conflicts.side_b_position: Originate land-use work program items at the JCCPC because planning jurisdiction is shared with the County.
side_b_arguments: Javiera Caballero noted land-use issues fall under both City Council and County Commissioners and recommended placing the item on the February JCCPC agenda first.
Mark-Anthony Middleton added that resolutions are aspirational rather than binding staff directives and noted any JCCPC work product still returns to full Council for debate.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; members aired preferences ahead of staff work-program scheduling.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Dec. 7, 2023
conflicts.issue: Extending ShotSpotter Pilot Contract for Three Months Pending Wilson Center Evaluation
conflicts.summary: Council members debated whether to keep ShotSpotter running for three months ($52,356) while the Wilson Center analyzes data from the already-concluding one-year pilot.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question extending the contract when no additional evaluation data will be collected and move the decision to the General Business Agenda for full public debate.
side_a_arguments: The Wilson Center evaluation is limited strictly to the 12-month pilot period ending December 14, so a 3-month extension yields no extra study data.
Extending an expired pilot without completed evaluation findings creates a slippery slope.
Public and council views warrant placing Item 11 on the General Business Agenda rather than Consent.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain continuity of ShotSpotter operations for three months rather than shutting sensors off mid-review.
side_b_arguments: ShotSpotter alerts have faster response times than 911 calls, led to arrests and gun recoveries, and alerted police when residents did not call 911.
No reports of aggressive policing from the pilot have materialized.
Deactivating sensors on December 14 while awaiting the report disrupts emergency response.
conflicts.resolution: Item 11 was pulled from Consent and placed on the December 18 General Business Agenda for a formal vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Dec. 19 2023
conflicts.issue: City Response to Calls for a Permanent Gaza Ceasefire Resolution
conflicts.summary: Following extensive public comments urging Durham to adopt UE150's permanent ceasefire resolution and redirect funds toward local wages and HEART, Mayor Leonardo Williams declined to adopt an externally authored resolution and noted Council lacked consensus on a single approach, proposing a dedicated four-hour council working session instead.
conflicts.side_a_position: Decline externally authored resolutions and convene a four-hour council session to draft an inclusive, council-authored statement or resolution.
side_a_arguments: Durham's municipal budget has no line item funding foreign wars.
Signing onto an externally authored resolution without council deliberation risks community division and broader repercussions.
Individual council members hold differing views, requiring structured space to reach a holistic response.
conflicts.side_b_position: Public speakers and community advocates demanded immediate introduction and passage of the UE150 ceasefire resolution.
side_b_arguments: Over 19,000 Palestinians have been killed and municipal resolutions apply political pressure on federal officials.
Durham has precedent taking international human rights stances such as opposing South African apartheid.
Taxpayer funds should be prioritized for $25/hour city worker wages and 24/7 HEART funding.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Council members voiced no objection to Mayor Williams's request to schedule a dedicated four-hour working session to craft a council response.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Jan 16, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Presided over by Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton while Mayor Leonardo Williams was in Washington, D.C., the January 16, 2024 regular meeting opened with the swearing-in of newly appointed Ward 3 Council Member Chelsea Cook, restoring Council to a full seven-member roster. Council approved Nate Baker's excused absence for the upcoming Thursday work session and unanimously adopted the consent agenda 6-0. In public hearings, Council unanimously adopted both the Teer Quarry UDO text amendment (TC2300003) and companion Eno River District A-2 watershed protection overlay map change (Z230030) to safeguard the new potable water intake, and continued the Cortez Drive Townhouses rezoning (Z220040) to February 5 so the applicant could meet with Council Member Cook.

agenda_items.title: Swearing-In of Ward 3 Council Member Chelsea Cook and Roll Call
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk administered the oath of office to Ward 3 Council Member-Designate Chelsea Cook following her appointment earlier that day, bringing the Council back to seven members. Roll call recorded Middleton, Nate Baker, Javiera Caballero, Cook, DeDreana Freeman, and Carl Rist present, with Mayor Leonardo Williams on an excused absence in Washington, D.C.

agenda_items.title: Human Trafficking Prevention Month Proclamation and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton read a proclamation declaring January 2024 Human Trafficking Prevention Month, presented to Kathy Nunes of The Bridge International. Council members welcomed Chelsea Cook, thanked MLK holiday event organizers, and approved Nate Baker's request for an excused absence from the January 18 work session; Middleton noted he would arrive late on January 18 while representing Durham during President Biden's visit, leaving DeDreana Freeman to preside.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1, 2, 4-18)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With no items pulled, Council unanimously adopted the consent agenda covering minutes, Environmental Affairs Board appointment, an Open Table Ministries emergency shelter contract, rear-mount ladder fire trucks, and major roadway, pavement preservation, sidewalk repair, traffic signal, and transit engineering contracts (Items 6-18).

agenda_items.title: Text Amendment: Teer Quarry (TC2300003)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff (Aaron Cain) presented UDO text revisions to Articles 4, 8, and 12 establishing watershed protection standards for the new Teer Quarry potable water supply intake, allowing existing lots of record to follow prior rules until redevelopment. Following a public hearing with no speakers, Council unanimously approved both the ordinance amendment and the NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Teer Quarry Watershed Overlay (Z230030)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: As the companion map change to Item 20, staff presented the reclassification of parcels within a half-mile of the Teer Quarry intake from Eno River Districts A and B into the Eno River District A-2 watershed protection overlay required by the NC Environmental Management Commission (already adopted by Durham County on Jan 8). Council asked about well/boring protections and unanimously approved the map change and consistency statement 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Cortez Drive Townhouses (Z220040)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff noted the Planning Commission recommended denial 8-4 in June 2023 and reported two new applicant proffers: at least 3% of units income-restricted at 80% AMI or below for 30 years and a $36,000 one-time donation to Durham Public Schools. The applicant's representative requested a continuance to February 5, 2024 to meet with newly seated Council Member Chelsea Cook, and Council kept the public hearing open to that date.

meetings.title: Special Durham City Council Meeting - Ward 3 Vacancy Jan 16 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At a 9:30 AM special meeting to fill the Ward 3 seat vacated when Leonardo Williams became mayor on December 4, 2023, the six seated council members initially deadlocked 3-3 between Sheila Huggins (backed by Williams, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Nate Baker) and Chelsea Cook (backed by Carl Rist, Javiera Caballero, and DeDreana Freeman). After debate over whether to use ranked-choice voting or allow a special election, Baker shifted his vote to Cook as a compromise to achieve the required four-vote majority. Following a 4-2 hand vote confirming Cook, Middleton noted the 4-2 count for the record before changing his vote to Cook as an act of goodwill, and Mayor Williams declared the selection unanimous.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Ward 3 Selection Procedure
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams called the special meeting to order with all six seated members present (Williams, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Nate Baker, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Carl Rist). He outlined that four votes were required to appoint a successor from the four finalists (Amanda Borer, Chelsea Cook, Sheila Huggins, and Chastin Swain), or else the vacancy would proceed to a special election.

agenda_items.title: Deliberation, Compromise, and Appointment of Chelsea Cook to Ward 3 Seat
agenda_items.discussion_summary: In first-round statements, Williams, Baker, and Middleton backed Sheila Huggins while Rist, Caballero, and Freeman backed Chelsea Cook, creating a 3-3 deadlock. After Freeman, Rist, and Baker expressed support for ranked-choice voting while Middleton opposed it and declined to name a second choice, Baker compromised to switch his vote to Cook, producing a 4-2 hand vote that Middleton subsequently joined as an act of goodwill so Cook's appointment was recorded unanimously.

votes.item_title: Appointment of Chelsea Cook to Fill the Vacant Ward 3 City Council Seat
votes.notes: Initially 3-3 (Huggins vs. Cook), then 4-2 for Cook on the hand vote (Middleton and Williams not voting for Cook initially), then changed to unanimous 6-0 at 00:26:08.
votes.discussion_detail: After an initial 3-3 split between Sheila Huggins (Williams, Middleton, Baker) and Chelsea Cook (Rist, Caballero, Freeman), Nate Baker compromised and shifted his vote to Cook to reach the four-vote threshold. A hand vote confirmed Cook 4-2 (Baker, Caballero, Freeman, Rist in favor), after which Middleton raised a point of order noting the 4-2 tally and changed his vote to Cook as an act of goodwill, and Mayor Williams declared the final vote unanimous for Cook.

meetings.title: Special Durham City Council: Ward 3 Vacancy Jan 10, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: The January 10, 2024 special City Council meeting was a dedicated public comment session allowing supporters to speak on behalf of the four finalists for the vacant Ward 3 council seat. With all six seated council members present and each finalist allocated up to 30 minutes of combined virtual and in-person testimony, supporters spoke in turn for Chastin Swain, Sheila Huggins, Chelsea Cook, and Amanda Borer. No deliberations or formal votes were taken, and Mayor Williams announced Council would reconvene at 9:30 AM on Tuesday, January 16 to cast its final selection vote, with the appointee to be sworn in that evening.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Candidate Support Hearing Format
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams called the candidate support meeting to order, the Clerk called the roll with all six seated members present, and Williams reminded attendees that Council would strictly listen while supporters spoke for up to 30 minutes per finalist across online and in-person speakers.

agenda_items.title: Public Support Comments for Chastin Swain
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Online and in-person supporters of Chastin Swain highlighted his collaborative leadership, governance and policy experience, humility, and commitment to climate and sustainability goals. disagreements.issue: East Club Gateway Voluntary Annexation and General Commercial Zoning (Z220062 / BDG220031)
disagreements.summary: Council split 2-4 over whether to annex 13.96 acres at East Club Boulevard and I-85 for a Commercial General textual development plan, weighing Transit Opportunity Area design standards and Comprehensive Plan fidelity against applying current UDO rules for a local developer.
disagreements.side_a_position: Deny the annexation and rezoning because the textual development plan falls short of Comprehensive Plan Transit Opportunity Area standards and leaves multifamily housing unprohibited.
side_a_arguments: Under Commercial General zoning without a housing prohibition, up to 90 residential units could still be built without addressing site constraints.
The proposal lacks strong urban design commitments beyond a partial build-to zone and could result in an auto-oriented strip center with a sea of parking inconsistent with the TOA place type.
Missing August Planning Commission comments and the need to uphold the newly adopted Comprehensive Plan ahead of the UDO rewrite warranted a no vote.
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve the annexation and rezoning as consistent with current UDO rules and the future Place Type Map.
side_b_arguments: The site is designated Transit Opportunity Area on the future place type map, and the applicant cannot use downtown design districts in the suburban tier until the UDO is rewritten.
Gander Development is a small, two-year-old local firm that offered an extensive list of prohibited nuisance uses, a perimeter fence, and a $15,000 affordable housing contribution.
Council should apply existing rules consistently rather than making anticipatory rulings against smaller local developers.
disagreements.resolution: Motion 1 for voluntary annexation and the utility extension agreement failed 2-4, ending consideration of the rezoning.

disagreements.summary: Following extensive public comments urging Durham to adopt UE150's permanent ceasefire resolution and redirect funds toward local wages and HEART, Mayor Leonardo Williams declined to adopt an externally authored resolution and noted Council lacked consensus on a single approach, proposing a dedicated four-hour council working session instead.
disagreements.side_a_position: Decline externally authored resolutions and convene a four-hour council session to draft an inclusive, council-authored statement or resolution.
side_a_arguments: Durham's municipal budget has no line item funding foreign wars.
Signing onto an externally authored resolution without council deliberation risks community division and broader repercussions.
Individual council members hold differing views, requiring structured space to reach a holistic response.
disagreements.side_b_position: Public speakers and community advocates demanded immediate introduction and passage of the UE150 ceasefire resolution.
side_b_arguments: Over 19,000 Palestinians have been killed and municipal resolutions apply political pressure on federal officials.
Durham has precedent taking international human rights stances such as opposing South African apartheid.

disagreements.side_a_position: Let the pilot contract expire as scheduled and await the Wilson Center evaluation before making any further commitment.
side_a_arguments: Extending the contract for three months yields no new evaluation data because the Wilson Center study only covers the completed 12-month pilot.
Community speakers cited false positives, missed shootings, and lack of proven crime reduction.
Resources should prioritize preventative community investments and evidence-based evaluation.
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve the $52,356 three-month extension to maintain continuity of gunfire detection until the Wilson Center report arrives in March.
side_b_arguments: Funds were already available within the Police Department budget and cutting service mid-review leaves shooting victims without alerts when 911 is not called.
Families and residents in high-gunfire areas reported valuing faster police response and recovered shell casings.
Keeping sensors active avoids operational disruption if Council decides to continue after reviewing the report.

disagreements.summary: While four members approved the Page Road / Greenwood annexation and rezoning after the developer doubled its housing fund proffer to $35,000, two members voted no due to the absence of on-site affordable units.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve annexation and PDR 7.827 rezoning for up to 70 townhouses with an increased $35,000 dedicated housing fund proffer.

disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose the rezoning and annexation because the development lacks on-site affordable units.
side_b_arguments: New townhome developments in Durham should include actual affordable units rather than relying solely on modest cash proffers.

disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt the clarifying text amendment immediately to align the UDO with 15 years of planning practice and insulate the City from litigation.
side_a_arguments: Reading §6.2.4.A's 12 aspirational purposes as mandatory makes conservation subdivisions legally impossible to approve.
Objective, measurable criteria in §6.2.4.H protect primary conservation areas without exposing the City to lawsuits.
Stronger environmental protections in Falls Lake and Southeast Durham were addressed through phased grading and belong in the UDO rewrite.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose the amendment over environmental enforcement concerns in Southeast Durham and dissatisfaction with removing purpose-statement safeguards.
side_b_arguments: Existing conservation subdivisions in Southeast Durham have caused severe sediment runoff into waterways.
Modifying the purpose-statement language before the Court of Appeals rules does not adequately strengthen environmental protection.
disagreements.resolution: The UDO text amendment passed 5-1 (DeDreana Freeman opposed), and the consistency statement passed 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 24: Continue Consolidated Annexation 5802 South Miami Boulevard Multi-Family to January 2, 2024
votes.notes: Public hearing remained open until January 2, 2024.
votes.discussion_detail: At the applicant's request to evaluate compliance with new UDO phasing, grading, and tree-coverage standards, Council agreed by unanimous consent to continue the public hearing on 5802 South Miami Boulevard to January 2, 2024.

votes.item_title: Item 25 (Motion 1): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Amendment for 618 Morehead Avenue (OI(D) to CG(D))
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously approved rezoning 618 Morehead Avenue from Office & Institutional with a development plan to Commercial General with a graphic development plan in the Morehead Hill Local Historic District, preserving the historic Greystone mansion.

votes.item_title: Item 25 (Motion 2): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for 618 Morehead Avenue
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously adopted the statutory consistency statement for the 618 Morehead Avenue rezoning.

votes.item_title: Item 26 (Motion 1): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Amendment for Oaks at Gray (321, 323, 325 Gray Ave)
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted 4-2 to rezone three parcels at 321-325 Gray Avenue from RU-M to RU-M with a textual development plan permitting up to eight townhouses, over objections from Nate Baker and DeDreana Freeman regarding density bonuses, displacement, and neighborhood design fit.

votes.item_title: Item 26 (Motion 2): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for Oaks at Gray
votes.discussion_detail: Moved by Javiera Caballero and seconded by Carl Rist, Council adopted the consistency statement for Oaks at Gray 5-1, with Nate Baker voting no.

votes.item_title: Accept Resignation of Leonardo Williams from Ward 3 City Council Seat
votes.discussion_detail: Moved by Carl Rist and properly seconded, Council unanimously accepted Mayor Leonardo Williams's formal resignation from his Ward 3 City Council seat.

disagreements.issue: Oaks at Gray Townhome Rezoning Density Bonus and Neighborhood Compatibility (321-325 Gray Ave)
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-2 over whether to rezone 0.435 acres in a predominantly single-family gentrifying neighborhood to allow eight market-rate townhouses instead of the five permitted by right.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the eight-townhouse rezoning as smaller, more attainable infill housing with off-street garage parking.
side_a_arguments: Building eight smaller 1,600-1,800 sq ft units yields lower price points than five larger townhomes allowed by right.
The project provides infill housing near downtown with garages and a small parking lot to address street parking concerns.
Local resident developers are investing in their first triangle project.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose granting three extra units by rezoning without using affordable housing density bonuses or single-family design commitments.
side_b_arguments: Granting extra units via rezoning undermines incentives for developers to use affordable housing density bonuses.
The property lies in a gentrifying neighborhood where $500k-$600k townhomes do not serve existing residents and exacerbate displacement.
The textual plan lacked design commitments to fit a predominantly single-family street and departed from the Established Residential place type.
disagreements.resolution: The zoning map change passed 4-2, and the consistency statement passed 5-1 (Nate Baker opposed).
